Anna (eng-runtime): quick sync — thinking about shrinking the operator surface for dedicated GPU pools. can we agree on a minimal API that still lets product shape cost vs SLA?
Mike S (orch): curious what "minimal" means here. do you mean fewer CRDs / no controller-side long-lived state?
Anna (eng-runtime): yeah. idea: move most policy decisions into a light-weight admission proxy + a tiny reconciler that only owns pool lifecycle, not per-tenant quotas. operator should be mostly stateless so upgrades are safe.
Jess R (sre): stateless admission proxy sounds attractive for stability. question: where do we keep warmup credit accounting and burst caps? we need sources of truth for costing and throttles.
Mike S (orch): proposal: keep accounting in the centralized billing ledger (external service) and have the admission proxy fetch ephemeral tokens. reconciler only syncs pool geometry (node sets, labels).
Tom L (product): from product side we need per-tenant SLO tiers (low-cost, standard, premium). each tier must map to a deterministic admission strategy so customer experience is predictable.
Anna (eng-runtime): mapping idea: tier -> lane config (max concurrent, prewarm window, fallback-model). config stored in config-service; admission proxy loads lanes and enforces.
Jess R (sre): fallback-models are crucial — when premium pool is saturated we should auto-fall back to compatible hosted variant. that's an operational must. also want observable counters for fallback frequency.
Mike S (orch): agree. Also want a simple backpressure signal for autoscaler: admission should emit a short expiry token when requests are queueing; controller uses token pressure to scale more aggressively. keeps operator simple.
Anna (eng-runtime): exact. token pressure + node-pending-count metrics should be enough to avoid complex intent APIs. we avoid a big intent surface.
Tom L (product): what about burst lanes? customers expect occasional spikes. can we provide a small burst credit pool per tenant without blowing up operator complexity?
Mike S (orch): implement burst credits as a soft quota in the admission proxy that consults the billing service for balance. on exhaustion, degrade to rate limiting. no durable per-request state in operator.
Jess R (sre): race conditions: two proxies could grant credits simultaneously. use an optimistic decrement API in billing service with a short TTL reservation. retries on conflict. keep admission idempotent.
Anna (eng-runtime): that keeps operator code readable. I can draft the admission proto:
```
POST /admit
body: { tenant_id, lane, requested_slots, trace_id }
resp: { approved_slots, expiry_ts, fallback_hint }
```

Mike S (orch): nice. small and testable. reconciler only handles pool health and node labels — scaling decisions come purely from autoscaler which watches token-pressure and pool-utilization metrics.
Tom L (product): can we guarantee cost explainability? customers will ask why they were billed for bursts. need trace_id propagated to billing and logs.
Jess R (sre): add a thin tracing header across the proxy -> billing -> autoscaler. OrchBot will also ingest traces for debugging.
OrchBot: deploy queued: admission-proxy/feature/minimal-surface -> staging at 2026-03-23T09:12:00Z :rocket:
Anna (eng-runtime): next steps: I'll open a short RFC with the admission proto + billing contract. Mike, can you sketch the reconciler scope? Jess, can you list required metrics/alerts? Tom, want to review lane configs for tiers.
Mike S (orch): yep will put a PR sketch by EOD.
Jess R (sre): metrics: pool_util_pct, queued_token_pressure, fallback_rate_{tier}, burst_credit_consumption, admission_latency_p50/95. alerts on persistent fallback_rate > 0.5% for 5m.
Tom L (product): I'll draft tier-to-lane mapping and some customer-facing docs for behavior guarantees.
Anna (eng-runtime): great — keeping operator tiny should let us ship faster and iterate on cost controls without risking cluster liveness. thanks all. :thumbsup:
